original_text: Historical Basis of Knowledge¨Following Mendel’s studies on heredity in the 1800’s scientists through the early 1900’s knew certain facts about genetic information.¨Mid-20thcentury, scientists knew genetic material:¤Able to store information for structure, development, metabolism¤Stable so it can be replicated with high accuracy¤Able to undergo rare changes called mutationsto provide genetic variability necessary for evolutionnRequirements for genetic material
explanation: Following Gregor Mendel's heredity studies in the 1800s, scientists by the mid-20th century had established specific criteria that any candidate for genetic material must meet. The three essential requirements for genetic material are: first, it must be able to store information needed for an organism's structure, development, and metabolism; second, it must be stable so that it can be replicated with high accuracy during cell division; and third, it must be capable of undergoing rare changes (mutations) to provide the genetic variability necessary for evolution.

It must be composed of exactly 20 different amino acids.
questions.exp: Option D is correct because mid-20th-century requirements did not state the material must be made of amino acids (in fact, this was a debate between protein and DNA). Options A, B, and C are incorrect because they represent the three requirements explicitly listed on the slide: storing information, high accuracy stability for replication, and susceptibility to rare mutations.

questions.q: Why did scientists determine that the genetic material must be capable of undergoing rare changes (mutations)?
opts: To prevent replication from occurring.
To ensure that offspring are identical clones of their parents.
To provide the genetic variability necessary for evolution.
To destroy harmful bacterial capsules.
questions.exp: Option C is correct because the slide states that mutations provide the genetic variability necessary for evolution. Option A is incorrect as stability/replication is a separate requirement. Option B is incorrect because mutations introduce variations, making offspring non-identical. Option D is unrelated to the requirement.

original_text: Historical Basis -GriffithLate 1920s England: Frederick Griffith studying S. pneumonia¤Causes lung disease pneumonia in mammals¤Non-infectious strain¤Infectious (virulent) strain¨Virulent strainsurrounded by polysaccharide capsule; protects from body’s defenses; grows in colonies with smooth edges (S strain)¨Non-virulent strain lacks capsule; grows in colonies with rough edges (R strain)¨Experimented with bacteria in mice to investigate transfer of hereditary information in bacteria
explanation: In the late 1920s in England, Frederick Griffith studied the bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae, which causes the lung disease pneumonia in mammals. He worked with two strains: an infectious (virulent) strain and a non-infectious (non-virulent) strain. The virulent strain is surrounded by a polysaccharide capsule that protects the bacterium from the host body's immune defenses, and it grows in colonies with smooth edges, earning it the name 'S strain.' In contrast, the non-virulent strain lacks this protective capsule and grows in colonies with rough edges, known as the 'R strain.' Griffith experimented with these bacteria in mice to investigate whether and how hereditary information could be transferred between bacterial cells.

original_text: Historical Basis -Avery¨Early 1940’s America: Oswald Avery sought to determine whether transforming agentfrom Griffith’s experiment was protein, RNA or DNA¨Enzymeswere used to destroy each of the 3 molecules in heat-killed S cells¤Protease: destroys protein(experiment 1)¤RNase: destroys RNA(experiment 2)¤DNase: destroys DNA(experiment 3)¨Mixed experimental batches of heat-killed S cells with live R cells and injected into mice¨Findings:¤Cells missing protein and RNA were still able to transform R cells: mice died¤Cells missing DNA could NOT transform R cells: mice lived¨Conclusion: DNAis the molecule responsiblefor transformation of bacteria
explanation: In the early 1940s in America, Oswald Avery set out to identify the chemical identity of the transforming agent from Griffith's experiment, specifically evaluating whether it was protein, RNA, or DNA. He used selective enzymes to destroy these molecules in heat-killed S (smooth, virulent) cells: Protease to destroy protein, RNase to destroy RNA, and DNase to destroy DNA. He then mixed each treated batch of heat-killed S cells with live R (rough, non-virulent) cells and injected them into mice. He observed that R cells mixed with heat-killed S cells missing protein or RNA were still successfully transformed, causing the mice to die. However, the mixture missing DNA could not transform the R cells, and the mice lived. Avery concluded that DNA is the molecule responsible for the transformation of bacteria, establishing it as the transforming agent.

original_text: Historical Basis –Hershey-Chase¨Early 1950’s America: Chase & Hershey sought to determinewhether DNA or protein was hereditary materialtransferred by viruses entering a bacterium¤Bacteriophage (phage): virus that infects bacteria¨Grew phage in presence of radioactive sulfur (35S) to label proteins¨Grew phage in presence of radioactive phosphorus (32P) to label DNA¨Allowed labeled phage to infect bacteria¨Used a blender to remove phage coats from cells¨Used a centrifuge to separate phage from bacteria¨Findings:¤Radioactive sulfur present in supernatant (viruses) not bacterial cell pellet¤Radioactive phosphorus present in bacterial cell pellet, notsupernatant¨Conclusion:¤DNAis the hereditary material of viruses¨Hershey Chase Visualized
explanation: In the early 1950s in America, Martha Chase and Alfred Hershey aimed to determine if DNA or protein was the hereditary material transferred by viruses. They used bacteriophages (phages), which are viruses that infect bacteria. They labeled phage proteins using radioactive sulfur (35S) and labeled phage DNA using radioactive phosphorus (32P). After allowing these labeled phages to infect bacteria, they used a blender to disrupt and remove empty phage coats from the cell surface and a centrifuge to separate the heavier bacteria (pellet) from the lighter viral coats (supernatant). They found that radioactive sulfur (35S) remained in the supernatant, whereas radioactive phosphorus (32P) was found within the bacterial pellet. This demonstrated that phage DNA, and not protein, was injected into the host bacteria, concluding that DNA is the hereditary material of viruses.

Sulfur makes the viral coat heavy enough to be separated by the blender.
Sulfur glows in the dark, allowing the researchers to see the viruses.
questions.exp: Option B is correct because sulfur is present in proteins (specifically in certain amino acids like cysteine and methionine) but is not found in DNA. This allows selective labeling of proteins. Option A is incorrect because phosphorus, not sulfur, is in the DNA backbone. Options C and D are incorrect descriptions.

opts: Radioactive sulfur (35S)
Radioactive phosphorus (32P)
Both 35S and 32P
Neither radioactive isotope
questions.exp: Option B is correct because the slide states: 'Radioactive phosphorus present in bacterial cell pellet, not supernatant.' Option A is incorrect because radioactive sulfur was in the supernatant. Options C and D are incorrect.

original_text: Historical Basis –Watson, Crick, Wilkins, & Franklin¨After DNA was determined to be hereditary material –next challenge: determine its structure¨Maurice Wilkins, Rosalind Franklinpurifiedand crystallized DNA, used a technique called X-ray diffractionto image it¨James Watson, Francis Crick used this information to propose a model for DNA structure in 1953¤Publicationin Nature: 1 page long with 1 hand drawn image of the structure¤Won Nobel Prizein Medicine, 1963, along with Wilkinsfor the discovery¤Franklin died from radiation exposure before award was given, but is recognized for producing the famous image that led to the discovery of the structure¨Proposed structure:¤2 chains wrapped around each other to form a double helix (winding, spiral staircase)¤Also proposed a mechanismforreplicationof DNA
explanation: After DNA was identified as the hereditary material, the next major challenge in molecular biology was to determine its molecular structure. Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin purified and crystallized DNA, using a technique called X-ray diffraction to capture its physical shape. James Watson and Francis Crick then used Franklin's and Wilkins's imaging data to build a model for the structure of DNA in 1953, which they published in a brief, one-page article in the journal Nature that featured a single hand-drawn diagram. For their discoveries, Watson, Crick, and Wilkins were awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1963 (according to the course slide). Rosalind Franklin passed away due to radiation exposure before the award was given, but she is highly recognized for producing the famous X-ray diffraction image that made the double helix model possible. The proposed DNA structure consists of two strands wrapped around each other in a double helix, resembling a winding spiral staircase, and it also suggests a mechanism for DNA replication.

explanation: DNA is a nucleic acid composed of two long complementary chains (strands) of repeating subunits called nucleotides. Each nucleotide itself consists of three essential parts: a 5-carbon sugar called deoxyribose, a phosphate group (PO4), and a nitrogenous base (which contains carbon and nitrogen and acts as a base by accepting hydrogen ions). There are four nitrogenous bases in DNA: adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine. The alternating sugar and phosphate molecules form the outer 'handrails' or the sugar-phosphate backbone of the DNA molecule. The nucleotides along a single strand are linked together by covalent bonds known as phosphodiester bonds, which connect the phosphate group of one nucleotide to the deoxyribose sugar of the next. Each complete turn of the DNA double helix contains approximately 10 nucleotides.

explanation: While the sugar and phosphate group components are identical across all DNA nucleotides, the nitrogenous bases differ. There are four types of nitrogenous bases in DNA: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), and thymine (T). Each base has a unique chemical structure, but they are all composed of carbon rings containing nitrogen groups. Based on their ring structure, they are classified into two groups: purines and pyrimidines. Purines are bases with a double-ring structure, which include adenine and guanine. Pyrimidines are bases with a single-ring structure, which include thymine and cytosine.

original_text: Complementary Bases¨American biochemist Chargoffobserved in a sample of DNA:¤% of A equals % of T; % of C equals % of G¨Led to development of base pairing rules, aka Chargoff’srules¤C on one strand always pairs with G on other¤A on one strand always pairs with T on other¤Pairs called complementary base pairs¨Pairs contain one purine; one pyrimidine¨Because of this:¤Order of bases on one strand is complementary to order of bases on other strand¤Order of bases known as base sequence, or DNA sequence¨Complementary base pairing important to DNA structure¤Hydrogen bonding holds strands together¤Complementary structure explains how DNA can be replicated before cell divisionnOne strand of DNA serves as template for formation of new complementary strand
explanation: American biochemist Erwin Chargaff observed that in any sample of DNA, the percentage of adenine (A) is equal to the percentage of thymine (T), and the percentage of cytosine (C) is equal to the percentage of guanine (G). This key finding led to the development of base pairing rules, known as Chargaff's rules, which specify that adenine on one strand always pairs with thymine on the opposite strand, and cytosine always pairs with guanine. These pairs are referred to as complementary base pairs, and each pair consists of one double-ring purine and one single-ring pyrimidine. Consequently, the order of bases on one strand is completely complementary to the order of bases on the other. This sequence of bases is referred to as the base sequence or DNA sequence. Complementary base pairing is critical to DNA's structure and function because hydrogen bonds between the complementary bases hold the two strands together. Furthermore, this complementary structure explains the mechanism of DNA replication prior to cell division: one strand can serve as a physical template for synthesis of a new complementary strand.

original_text: DNA Replication¨Process by which DNA is copied in a dividing cell¤Mitosis, meiosis or binary fission¨The 2 nucleotide strands of the helix separate (melt)¨Complementary strands: each serves as a template for a new daughter strand1.Helicasesseparate/unwind the DNA strands1.Break the H-bonds between bases2.Y-shaped region results: replication fork2.DNA polymerases bind to DNA molecule, add complementary nucleotides, catalyze formation of covalent bond between nucleotides1.H-bonds spontaneously form between complementary bases between new and old strand3.DNA polymerases complete replication; fall off¨Result: 2 separate, identical DNA molecules ready for cell division
explanation: DNA replication is the process by which a cell copies its DNA prior to division (whether through mitosis, meiosis, or prokaryotic binary fission). The process begins when the two complementary strands of the double helix separate (sometimes called 'melting'). Because they are complementary, each original strand serves as a template for synthesizing a new daughter strand. The replication process proceeds in three main steps: First, enzymes called helicases separate and unwind the DNA strands by breaking the hydrogen bonds holding the base pairs together. This unwinding forms a Y-shaped region called the replication fork. Second, enzymes called DNA polymerases bind to the separated DNA strands, add complementary nucleotides, and catalyze the formation of covalent bonds between the newly added nucleotides. Meanwhile, hydrogen bonds spontaneously form between the complementary bases of the new and template strands. Third, once the replication is complete, the DNA polymerases release and fall off the DNA molecule. The final result is two separate, identical DNA molecules, each ready for cell division.

original_text: DNA Replication¨Each new DNA double helix: 1 strand from original molecule; 1 strand newly synthesized¤Known as semi-conservative replication¨Synthesis occurs in different directions on each strand¨As replication fork moves along DNA template molecule, synthesis of one strand follows¤Synthesis occurs from 5’-3’; each strand of DNA has a different directionality. n5’-3’, compliment is 3’-5’ when lined up next to each other¨Synthesis on other strand moves in opposite direction; away from replication fork; leaves gaps in new strand¤Known as Okazaki fragments¤Joined together by DNA ligase
explanation: When DNA replication is complete, each new DNA double helix consists of one strand conserved from the original parental molecule and one newly synthesized strand. This mode of replication is called semi-conservative replication. Because the two strands of the DNA double helix run anti-parallel (one is 5'-3', and the other is 3'-5'), replication occurs in different directions on each strand. DNA polymerase can only synthesize new DNA in the 5' to 3' direction. On one template strand, synthesis occurs continuously in the same direction as the moving replication fork. On the opposite strand, synthesis must move in the opposite direction (away from the replication fork), which is done in short, discontinuous segments. These segments are called Okazaki fragments. Once synthesized, these fragments are joined together into a continuous strand by the enzyme DNA ligase.

explanation: DNA replication is an extremely accurate process, averaging only one error for every billion nucleotides copied. This high fidelity is due to the proofreading function of DNA polymerase. As it builds the new strand, DNA polymerase reads the newly synthesized DNA to ensure that bases are paired correctly. If an error is detected, the enzyme removes the incorrect nucleotide and inserts the correct one. However, some errors slip through. An unrepaired replication error results in a base sequence that differs from the parent DNA. Any change in the nucleotide sequence is called a mutation, which can alter a gene and disrupt normal cellular functions. In addition to replication errors, DNA can be damaged by external factors like chemicals and UV radiation from the sun. If these mutations are not repaired, they can potentially lead to cancer.

explanation: Most DNA mutations occur during the process of replication, though they can also be caused by other external factors. The consequences of mutations vary widely. Some mutations provide an advantage to the cell or organism, leading to adaptation and driving evolution. Other mutations cause no change in the organism's physical characteristics (phenotype) and are called silent mutations. However, many mutations are deleterious. They can result in a mis-functioning or completely non-functional protein, causing genetic diseases. When mutations occur in genes that regulate the cell cycle—such as tumor suppressor genes or oncogenes—they can disrupt cell division controls and lead to cancer.

explanation: RNA is a nucleic acid composed of nucleotides, but it differs from DNA in four fundamental ways: 1) RNA contains the 5-carbon sugar ribose, whereas DNA contains deoxyribose; 2) RNA contains the nitrogenous base uracil instead of thymine (uracil pairs with adenine, just as thymine does in DNA); 3) RNA is single-stranded, although it can fold and base-pair with itself in short segments to form double-stranded regions; and 4) RNA is short, typically only the length of one gene, whereas DNA molecules are extremely long and contain thousands of genes. original_text: Transcription¨Process by which genetic instructions are transcribed (re-written) into RNA molecule –produces mRNA Molecule¨Occurs in nucleus of eukaryotes; nucleoid region of prokaryotes1.RNA polymerase binds to promoter on DNA template molecule¤Promoter:specific DNA sequence that serves as recognition site for RNA polymerase to bind and initiate transcription¤DNA strands are separated and unwound2.RNA polymerase adds free RNA nucleotides complementary to nucleotides on DNA template¤Complementary base pairing determines sequence of new RNA molecule based on DNA template¤Only a specific region, gene, is transcribed. 5’à3’ direction -elongation¤One DNA strand used as template; as RNA polymerase moves past, DNA rewound3.RNA polymerase reaches termination signal; DNA sequence that marks end of gene¤Stop signal; RNA polymerase releases template DNA and newly synthesized RNA molecule¨New transcript can be started as soon as the promoter is free
explanation: Transcription is the process of re-writing DNA instructions into an RNA molecule (specifically creating mRNA). This takes place in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells and the nucleoid region of prokaryotes. The process has three main steps: 1) Initiation: The enzyme RNA polymerase binds to a specific DNA sequence called a promoter, which serves as a recognition site to start transcription, causing the DNA strands to separate and unwind. 2) Elongation: RNA polymerase moves along one of the DNA strands (acting as a template) in the 5' to 3' direction, adding free complementary RNA nucleotides. The sequence of the new RNA is dictated by complementary base pairing with the DNA template. As the polymerase passes, the DNA helix rewinds. 3) Termination: When RNA polymerase reaches a termination signal (a specific DNA sequence marking the end of the gene), it releases the template DNA and the newly completed RNA transcript. A new transcription process can begin at the promoter as soon as the previous RNA polymerase leaves the promoter area.

original_text: mRNA Processing¨Newly formed pre-mRNA must undergo processing before it leaves the nucleus¤mRNA receives a capat its 5’ endnModified Guanine. Tells a ribosome where to attached when translation begins¤Poly-A Tail –150-200 adenine (A) added to 3’ end. nFacilitates transport out of nucleusnHelps initiate loading into ribosomenDelays degradation of mRNA by hydrolytic enzymes¤Contains mix of intronsand exonsnIntron–Non-protein coding region of pre-mRNAnExon–Protein coding region of pre-mRNAnTo create the final mature mRNA, a spliceosomewill cut out the intron regions
explanation: In eukaryotic cells, newly transcribed pre-mRNA must undergo mRNA processing within the nucleus before it can be exported to the cytoplasm. This processing involves three key modifications: first, a cap consisting of a modified guanine nucleotide is added to the 5' end of the mRNA, which signals the ribosome where to attach when translation starts. Second, a Poly-A Tail—consisting of 150 to 200 adenine nucleotides—is added to the 3' end. This tail facilitates mRNA transport out of the nucleus, helps initiate ribosome loading, and delays the degradation of the mRNA by hydrolytic enzymes. Third, the pre-mRNA contains a mixture of exons (coding regions) and introns (non-coding regions). A molecular complex called a spliceosome cuts out the introns and splices the exons together, producing a mature mRNA ready for translation.

original_text: Introns¨Role was unknown for a long time¤Alternative mRNA SplicingnOne mRNA can lead to multiple different products depending on which exons are left in or out of final mRNA product. ¤microRNAsnSmall molecules involved in regulating translation of mRNAsnWill bind with mRNA and prevent translation¤May play roll in crossing-overin meiosis –exon shuffling
explanation: For a long time, the biological role of introns was unknown, but scientists have discovered several important functions. Introns enable alternative mRNA splicing, a process where exons can be selectively included or excluded from the final mature mRNA transcript, allowing a single gene to code for multiple different protein products. In addition, introns often contain genetic sequences for microRNAs, which are small RNA molecules that regulate gene expression by binding to target mRNAs and preventing their translation. Furthermore, introns may facilitate crossing-over during meiosis by promoting 'exon shuffling,' which can generate new combinations of genes and proteins.

original_text: Genetic Code¨Gene expression: amino acids assembled based on instructions encoded in sequence of nucleotides in mRNA¨Genetic code: rules that relate how sequence of bases in nucleotides correspond to particular amino acid¤3 adjacent nucleotides in mRNA specify an amino acid in a polypeptidenKnown as a codon¤1 codon known as START; always found at the beginning of mRNA sequence; codes for amino acid methioninenAUG¤3 codons known as STOP; signifies end of polypeptide moleculenUAA, UAG, UGA¨Code is nearly universal among organisms¤Supports the idea all organisms came from common ancestor¨61 codons code for 20 amino acids + 3 STOP¨No codon codes for more than one amino acid; some amino acids encoded by 2 or more codons¤Code is unambiguous and redundant
explanation: Gene expression is the process where amino acids are assembled into polypeptides based on genetic instructions carried by the nucleotide sequence in mRNA. The genetic code consists of rules that translate this nucleotide sequence into specific amino acids. Every group of three adjacent nucleotides in mRNA is called a codon, which specifies one amino acid. The code features one START codon, AUG, which is located at the beginning of the mRNA sequence and codes for the amino acid methionine. There are three STOP codons (UAA, UAG, and UGA) that signal the end of a polypeptide chain. The genetic code is nearly universal across all living organisms, suggesting a common evolutionary origin. Of the 64 possible codons, 61 code for the 20 amino acids (including the AUG start codon), and the remaining 3 are stop codons. The genetic code is unambiguous (no single codon codes for more than one amino acid) and redundant (several different codons can code for the same amino acid).

original_text: Translation –Role of rRNA/Ribosomes ¨rRNA codes for 2 ribosomal subunits¤Large and small subunit make up all ribosomes. ¤Join together at start of translation¤Ribosomes can remain in cytoplasm or attached to ER¨Ribosome has a binding site for mRNA, and 3 binding sites for tRNA¤E, P , & A sites in large subunitnE –Exit –location where the used tRNAexitsnP –Protein –where tRNAbound to amino acid is processed to elongate the protein chainnA –Amino Acid –where next amino acid anticodon enters and waits to move to P site¨Enzyme Ribozyme helps create peptide bond between neighboring amino acids
explanation: During translation, transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules transport amino acids to the ribosomes. A tRNA molecule is a single-stranded RNA chain folded into a flat shape resembling a clover leaf. There is at least one specific tRNA for each of the 20 amino acids, and the amino acid binds to the 3' end of the tRNA. The opposite end of the tRNA contains an anticodon—a three-nucleotide sequence complementary to the 5' to 3' codon on mRNA. Interestingly, there are fewer tRNA molecules (only about 40) than codons. To explain this, Francis Crick proposed the Wobble Hypothesis, which suggests that the base-pairing rules are relaxed at the third position of the codon. This wobble allows the first two positions of the tRNA anticodon to pair with up to four different codons that differ only at their third base. This flexibility is a primary reason the genetic code is described as degenerate, and specific enzymes are required to link each tRNA to its corresponding amino acid.

original_text: Translation¨Process by which protein is constructed from mRNA instructions; uses all forms of RNA; occurs in cytosol1.Initiation -2 ribosomal subunits, tRNA, mRNA join together ¤Enzymes attach corresponding amino acid to end of each tRNAmolecule according to genetic code¤Opposite end of tRNAcontains anticodon: 3 nucleotide sequence that is complementary to codon in mRNA¤Ex: tRNAwith anticodon UAC will bind to mRNA codon AUG and carry amino acid methionine (start)2.Next tRNApairs its anticodon with mRNA codon¤Ribosome detaches methionine from first tRNA; forms peptide bond between it and next amino acid¤First tRNAleaves ribosome¤Ribosome moves to next codon in sequence3.Elongation-Polypeptide chain continues to grow¤tRNAscome in carrying amino acids¤Translocation-Growing chain transferred from one tRNAto amino acid attached to next tRNA4.Termination-Ribosome reaches STOP codon; newly synthesized polypeptide is released5.Translational components come apart; free to translate another mRNA
explanation: Translation is the cellular process by which proteins are synthesized from the instructions on an mRNA molecule. This process occurs in the cytosol and requires all three forms of RNA (mRNA, tRNA, and rRNA). Translation proceeds in five stages: 1) Initiation: The small and large ribosomal subunits, mRNA, and an initiator tRNA join together. Specific enzymes attach corresponding amino acids to their respective tRNAs. The anticodon of the tRNA binds to the complementary codon on mRNA; for example, an initiator tRNA with the anticodon UAC binds to the start codon AUG and carries the amino acid methionine. 2) Next tRNA pairing: A second tRNA binds to the adjacent mRNA codon. The ribosome releases the methionine from the first tRNA and catalyzes a peptide bond between it and the second amino acid. The first tRNA exits, and the ribosome advances. 3) Elongation: As the ribosome translocates along the mRNA, new tRNAs enter carrying amino acids, and the growing polypeptide chain is continuously transferred to the newly arrived amino acid. 4) Termination: When the ribosome reaches a STOP codon, translation stops and the completed polypeptide is released. 5) Disassembly: The translational components dissociate and are recycled to translate other mRNA molecules.

explanation: The entire sequence of the human genome is known, encompassing approximately 3.2 billion base pairs organized across 23 chromosomes. To analyze and extract information from this massive amount of data, scientists rely on bioinformatics, a field that applies computer science, statistics, and mathematics to biological systems. Bioinformatics allows researchers to rapidly compare diverse DNA sequences and interpret genomic data to map the locations of specific genes on chromosomes. Although we know the sequences, scientists are still working to determine when and where cells express the proteins coded by the estimated 20,000 to 30,000 genes in our genome. Understanding these gene sequences and their regulatory pathways is vital for diagnosing, treating, and preventing genetic disorders, cancer, and infectious diseases.

explanation: Gene regulation refers to the processes by which cells turn specific genes on or off (controlling whether they are expressed or not). This regulation is necessary because cells do not need all of their genes transcribed and translated into proteins at all times. By controlling gene expression, cells can conserve resources and produce specific gene products only when they are needed. The mechanisms and structures of gene regulation differ significantly between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

original_text: Prokaryotic Regulation¨Prokaryotic DNA is normally less complex than eukaryotic¤Genes for a certain pathway are all grouped together so that they are transcribed at the same time¤These are termed Structural Genes¨Gene regulation in prokaryotes controlled by repressors, and the entire gene encoding region known as an Operon¨Some operons in always on state unless regulated, and others in always off unless regulated
explanation: Prokaryotic DNA is generally less complex than eukaryotic DNA. In prokaryotes, genes that function together in a metabolic pathway are grouped together on the chromosome so they can be transcribed simultaneously into a single mRNA molecule. These grouped genes are known as structural genes. In prokaryotes, gene expression is controlled by DNA-binding proteins called repressors, and the entire functional unit of DNA containing these clustered genes and their regulatory sequences is called an operon. Some operons are default-on (expressed continuously unless specifically turned off by regulation), while others are default-off (not expressed unless specifically turned on).

explanation: An operon consists of several specific DNA elements that work together to control gene expression: 1) Regulator gene: Located outside the operon itself, it codes for DNA-binding proteins that act as repressors, controlling whether the operon is active or inactive. 2) Promoter: A short DNA sequence situated before the structural genes where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription. 3) Operator: A segment of DNA located next to or following the promoter. A repressor protein can bind to the operator; when the operator is bound by a repressor, RNA polymerase is physically blocked from binding to the promoter, preventing transcription. 4) Structural genes: The actual genes within the operon that code for the functional enzymes and proteins of the pathway.

explanation: The trp operon is a repressible operon, which is normally in an 'on' state (active) unless regulated. Repressible operons are typically associated with anabolic (biosynthetic) pathways. explanation: The structure of chromatin plays a major role in gene regulation. Euchromatin is a loosely compacted form of DNA, making genes accessible to RNA polymerase for transcription. In contrast, heterochromatin is highly compacted DNA that is transcriptionally inactive. The histone proteins around which DNA wraps are directly involved in this structural regulation. Histones have tail regions that can be chemically modified: in heterochromatin, these tails have methyl groups (-CH3) added (methylated), promoting tight compaction. In euchromatin, these tails have acetyl groups (-COCH3) added (acetylated), which loosens the histone-DNA interaction. A molecular machine called the Chromatin Remodeling Complex can then push aside these acetylated histones, clearing the path for transcription to proceed.

original_text: 1) Chromatin Structure Regulation¨Heterochromatin is not transcribed¤In genetic females, one X chromosome is inactivated in a process called X-inactivation –creates a Barr BodynOne gets highly condensed, and unavailable for transcriptionnMeans genetic males and females will produce same amount of gene products from X chromosomenX chromosome inactivated differs from cell to cellnCan result in mosaic expression with some heterozygous genes
explanation: Heterochromatin is highly condensed and cannot be transcribed. In genetic female mammals (who inherit two X chromosomes), one of the two X chromosomes is permanently shut down in a process called X-inactivation, forming a highly condensed structure known as a Barr Body. This inactivation ensures dosage compensation, meaning that genetic males (who have only one X chromosome) and females produce equivalent amounts of gene products from X-linked genes. The choice of which X chromosome is inactivated (maternal or paternal) occurs randomly and independently in each embryonic cell. Consequently, if a female is heterozygous for a gene on the X chromosome, she will show a mosaic pattern of expression, where different cells express different alleles.

explanation: Epigenetic inheritance refers to variations in inheritance patterns that are not caused by changes in the underlying DNA sequence, but rather by chemical modifications such as methylation. Specifically, when histone proteins associated with a gene become methylated, the DNA itself can also undergo methylation, which acts to silence gene expression. A specific form of epigenetic regulation is genomic imprinting, which is the process where alleles from either the mother or the father (but not both) are methylated during gamete formation. If an inherited allele is methylated, it is transcriptionally silenced. The gene itself is completely normal in sequence, but its expression is blocked solely due to this methylation imprint.

explanation: Transcriptional control is the most critical level of gene regulation in eukaryotic cells. It is significantly more complicated than in prokaryotes. Crucially, eukaryotic cells do not contain operons. Instead, they rely on various proteins called transcription factors (T-factors) to regulate gene expression. These transcription factors assist RNA polymerase in binding to a gene's promoter. Many promoters require multiple transcription factors before transcription can begin. In addition, some genes require a transcription activator to assist in initiation. Regulatory DNA sequences called enhancers, which can be located far away on the chromosome, may need to be bound by transcription factors to trigger a structural change (such as DNA looping) that allows transcription to start. Conversely, repressor proteins can bind to silencer regions near the promoter of a gene to halt transcription.

Option A is false. Option C is false because it is the 'Most critical level' of regulation. Option D is false because enhancers are 'located elsewhere on the chromosome.'

explanation: Post-transcriptional control occurs inside the nucleus after transcription is complete. It primarily involves alternative mRNA splicing and regulating the speed at which mRNA is exported from the nucleus. During alternative splicing, introns are removed and exons are joined together. By splicing these segments in different combinations, a single gene can produce multiple alternative mRNA transcripts, allowing eukaryotic DNA to code for far more protein products than the number of genes alone would suggest. However, if an intron is mistakenly left in the final mRNA product (which can then function as small nuclear RNA, or snRNA), the cell will destroy the defective mRNA before it can leave the nucleus.

explanation: Only about 1.5% of the total DNA in a cell actually codes for genes. For a long time, the other 98.5% of DNA was considered 'junk DNA.' However, it is now known that this non-coding region contains small RNA (sRNA) genes involved in genetic regulation. These sRNA molecules can alter the compaction of DNA so that genes are rendered inaccessible to transcription. This non-coding region is the source of microRNAs (miRNAs)—which are described on the slide as small pieces of DNA that bind to and dampen translation in the cytoplasm (note that miRNAs are functional RNA, but they originate from genomic DNA loci). It is also the source of small-interfering RNAs (siRNAs), which join with an enzyme to silence mRNA products, preventing them from being translated. Both miRNAs and siRNAs are currently utilized in gene therapy, a pioneering discovery that won the Nobel Prize in 2006.

explanation: Post-translational control regulates the activity of protein products after they have been synthesized. This is accomplished by controlling both their activation rate and their degradation rate. In terms of activation, many proteins are not immediately functional after translation. In terms of degradation, enzymes called proteases break down proteins. These proteases are sequestered within cell structures called proteasomes, described as a special type of lysosome. A protein is targeted for degradation when it is tagged by a signaling protein, indicating it should be transported to the proteasome for disassembly.

explanation: Gene mutations are classified as either spontaneous or induced. explanation: Gene mutations can be classified into point mutations and frameshift mutations. Point mutations involve a change in a single DNA nucleotide, which changes a single codon to a different codon in the transcript. The resulting effects on the protein vary; it may be rendered completely nonfunctional, have reduced functionality, or remain unaffected. In contrast, frameshift mutations involve the insertion or deletion of one or two nucleotides from DNA. Because codons are read in groups of three, inserting or deleting one or two bases shifts the entire reading frame downstream of the mutation, which always renders the protein nonfunctional. explanation: Cloning refers to the biological process of generating genetically identical copies of DNA, cells, or entire organisms. explanation: PCR has critical applications in analyzing DNA segments. One major technique is Short Tandem Repeat (STR) profiling, which determines the length of specific DNA fragments. These fragments are then separated using gel electrophoresis, which moves them through a gel matrix based on their size and charge (often called a 'torturous path' because of the gel matrix). explanation: Findings from the Human Genome Project revealed that humans possess approximately 20,500 genes, most of which code for proteins. original_text: Intro to Meiosis¨Process of nuclear division that reduces chromosome number in new cells to half original cell¨Meiosisproduces gametes –haploid reproductive cells ¤Human gametes: sperm and egg¤Each contain 1n chromosomes (23)¤Fusion of sperm & egg produces 2n zygotewith 46 chromosomes¨Cells still undergo G1, S and G2 phases of interphase in preparation of first division ¨Cells will divide twice:¤Diploid (2n) cells produce 4 haploid (1n) cells; rather than 2 diploid cells as in mitosis¨First cell division: meiosis I¨Second cell division: meiosis II
explanation: Meiosis is a form of nuclear division that reduces the chromosome number in the daughter cells to half of that in the parent cell. It produces gametes, which are haploid (1n) reproductive cells (sperm and egg in humans), each carrying 23 chromosomes. Fertilization, which is the fusion of a sperm and egg, forms a diploid (2n) zygote with 46 chromosomes. Prior to dividing, meiotic cells undergo interphase (G1, S, and G2 phases). Meiosis involves two successive cell divisions: meiosis I and meiosis II. As a result, a single diploid (2n) cell divides to produce four haploid (1n) daughter cells, in contrast to mitosis which yields two diploid cells.

explanation: Prophase I of meiosis introduces events not seen in mitosis. Chromosomes align with their homologues in a process called synapsis, forming a tetrad. original_text: Sexual Reproduction¨Production of offspring via meiosis and union of sperm and egg¨Offspring produced are genetically different from parent¤Genes are combined in new ways during meiosisnCrossing over and independent assortment¤Offspring contain unique combinations of parents’ genesnExcept for identical twins¨Evolutionary advantage of sexual reproduction:¤Enables species to rapidly adapt to new conditions¤Genetic variation leads to ‘survival of fittest’nOrganisms with most favorable traits survive to reproduce and pass on their traits¨Offspring from asexual reproduction are genetically identical to parent (clone)¤Offers no genetic diversity¤Simplest organisms
explanation: Sexual reproduction involves producing offspring through meiosis and the subsequent fusion (union) of sperm and egg gametes. Shuffling genetic material during meiosis via crossing-over and independent assortment combines genes in new ways, yielding offspring that are genetically distinct from their parents (with the exception of identical twins). The primary evolutionary benefit of sexual reproduction is that genetic variation allows species to rapidly adapt to new conditions, driving the survival of the fittest where organisms with favorable traits live to pass them on. Conversely, asexual reproduction produces genetically identical clones of the parent, which provides no genetic diversity and is typically limited to simpler organisms.

explanation: Crossing-over is a key mechanism in Meiosis I (written as 'Meiosis 1' on the slide) that increases genetic diversity. Usually, crossing-over and the subsequent segregation of chromosomes occur without complications. Consequently, chromosomes may fail to separate properly during meiosis, an error known as nondisjunction. Nondisjunction results in a gamete with a net gain or loss of a chromosome (+1 or -1).

explanation: Euploidy refers to having the correct, normal number of chromosomes characteristic of a species. Aneuploidy is an altered chromosome number resulting from nondisjunction. Secondary nondisjunction occurs during Meiosis II when sister chromatids fail to separate in one of the cells, resulting in two normal gametes.

explanation: Punnett squares are tables that list all possible genotypes resulting from a genetic cross. To set up a Punnett square, all possible sperm genotypes from one parent are lined up on one side, and all possible egg genotypes from the other parent are lined up on the other side. The possible zygote genotypes are filled in the grid. This tool allows the calculation of the probability of genotypes and phenotypes in the offspring. For example, if there is a 50% (or 1/2) chance of inheriting allele E and a 50% chance of inheriting e, the probability of offspring genotypes are: EE = 1/2 * 1/2 = 1/4, Ee = 1/4, eE = 1/4, and ee = 1/4.

questions.q: How is a Punnett square set up to calculate offspring genotypes?
opts: Sperm genotypes are placed inside the squares and egg genotypes are ignored.

questions.exp: Option B is correct because the chance of inheriting 'e' from one parent is 1/2, and from the other parent is 1/2. The joint probability is 1/2 * 1/2 = 1/4 (or 25%).

explanation: Genetic disorders are medical conditions resulting from alleles inherited from parents. An autosome is any chromosome other than a sex chromosome (X or Y). Genetic disorders caused by genes on autosomes are called autosomal disorders. Autosomal dominant disorders occur in individuals with genotype AA or Aa, while those with genotype aa are unaffected. original_text: Extending the Range of Mendelian Genetics¨Some traits are controlled by multiple alleles (multiple allelic traits)¨The gene exists in several allelic forms (but each individual only has two alleles)¨ABO blood types¤The alleles:nIA= A antigen on red blood cells, anti-B antibody in plasmanIB= B antigen on red blood cells, anti-A antibody in plasmani= Neither A nor B antigens on red blood cells, both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma¨The ABO blood type is also an example of codominance¤More than one allele is fully expressed¤Both IAand IBare expressed in the presence of the other
explanation: Some genetic traits are controlled by multiple alleles (multiple allelic traits), where the gene exists in several allelic forms in a population, although each individual only inherits two alleles. The ABO blood group system is a classic example of this. The alleles include IA (which encodes the A antigen on red blood cells and anti-B antibody in plasma), IB (which encodes the B antigen on red blood cells and anti-A antibody in plasma), and i (which encodes neither antigen, with both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in the plasma). ABO blood types also illustrate codominance, where both IA and IB alleles are fully expressed in a heterozygote (IAIB), meaning both A and B antigens are present.

original_text: Extending the Range of Mendelian Genetics¨Incomplete Dominance:¤Heterozygote has a phenotype intermediate between that of either homozygotenHomozygous red has red phenotypenHomozygous white has white phenotypenHeterozygote has pink (intermediate) phenotype¤Phenotype reveals genotype without a test cross
explanation: Incomplete dominance occurs when the heterozygote displays a phenotype that is intermediate between the phenotypes of the two homozygotes. For example, crossing a homozygous red flower with a homozygous white flower results in heterozygous offspring with pink flowers. Because of this, the phenotype of the individual directly reveals its genotype, eliminating the need for a testcross to determine the underlying alleles.

questions.q: What is the phenotypic outcome of a heterozygote in incomplete dominance?

questions.exp: Option C is correct because each genotype corresponds to a distinct, unique phenotype (e.g. AA is red, Aa is pink, aa is white), so the 'Phenotype reveals genotype without a test cross'.

original_text: Extending the Range of Mendelian Genetics¨Human examples of incomplete dominance:¤Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH)nHomozygotes for the mutant allele develop fatty deposits in the skin and tendons and may have heart attacks during childhoodnHeterozygotes may suffer heart attacks during early adulthoodnHomozygotes for the normal allele do not have the disorder
explanation: An example of incomplete dominance in humans is Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH). Homozygotes for the mutant allele develop fatty deposits in their skin and tendons, and they are at risk of having heart attacks during childhood. Heterozygotes have a milder form of the condition and may suffer heart attacks during early adulthood. Homozygotes for the normal allele do not have the disorder.

questions.q: How does Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH) demonstrate incomplete dominance in humans?
opts: Heterozygotes show no symptoms, while homozygotes die in childhood.

It only affects females, skipping males entirely.
The disease is only expressed if triggered by environmental pollutants.

questions.q: What are the clinical symptoms of individuals homozygous for the mutant allele in Familial Hypercholesterolemia?
opts: Spherical and fragile red blood cells.

Blue-purple coloration of the skin due to methemoglobin accumulation.
questions.exp: Option C is correct because the slide states mutant homozygotes: 'develop fatty deposits in the skin and tendons and may have heart attacks during childhood'.

original_text: Extending the Range of Mendelian Genetics¨Human examples of incomplete dominance:¤Incomplete penetrancenThe dominant allele may not always lead to the dominant phenotype in a heterozygotenMany dominant alleles exhibit varying degrees of penetrancenExample: polydactylynExtra digits on hands, feet,or bothnNot all individuals who inheritthe dominant polydactyly allele will exhibit the trait
explanation: Incomplete penetrance is a phenomenon where a dominant allele does not always lead to the expression of the dominant phenotype in a heterozygote. Many dominant alleles exhibit varying degrees of penetrance. An example of incomplete penetrance is polydactyly, which is characterized by extra digits on the hands, feet, or both. Not everyone who inherits the dominant polydactyly allele will actually develop extra digits.

questions.q: What is incomplete penetrance?

When genes on the X chromosome fail to segregate.

original_text: Extending the Range of Mendelian Genetics¨Pleiotropyoccurs when a single mutant gene affects two or more distinct and seemingly unrelated traits.¨Marfansyndrome is pleiotropic and results in the following phenotypes:¤disproportionately long arms, legs, hands, and feet¤a weakened aorta¤poor eyesightnAll seemingly unrelated, but due to the production of abnormal connective tissue resulting from a mutated fibrillin gene on chromosome 15 (FBN1)¨Sickle cell Anemia another example
explanation: Pleiotropy occurs when a single mutant gene affects two or more distinct and seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits. Marfan syndrome is a classic human example of a pleiotropic disorder, resulting in disproportionately long limbs, hands, and feet, a weakened aorta, and poor eyesight. These seemingly unrelated symptoms are all caused by the production of abnormal connective tissue due to a mutated fibrillin gene on chromosome 15 (specifically, the FBN1 gene). Sickle cell anemia is another example of a pleiotropic genetic disorder.

questions.q: What is pleiotropy?

When a gene mutation occurs only in somatic cells.

questions.q: What gene mutation on which chromosome causes the pleiotropic symptoms of Marfan syndrome?

original_text: Extending the Range of Mendelian Genetics¨Polygenic Inheritance:¤Occurs when a trait is governed by two or more genes having different alleles¤Each dominant allele has a quantitative effect on the phenotype¤These effects are additive¤Results in continuous variation of phenotypes within a population¤The traits may also be affected by the environment¤ExamplesnHuman skin colornHeightnEye color¤Disorders known to involve multiple genes having an effect include cleft lip, hypertension, diabetes, allergies and cancer
explanation: Polygenic inheritance occurs when a single trait is governed by two or more genes with different alleles. In this pattern, each dominant allele has a quantitative and additive effect on the phenotype. This results in continuous variation of the phenotypes within a population, rather than discrete categories. These traits are also typically influenced by the environment. Examples of polygenic traits in humans include skin color, height, and eye color. Disorders known to involve polygenic inheritance include cleft lip, hypertension, diabetes, allergies, and cancer.

explanation: In mammals, sex is determined by the X and Y chromosomes, where females are XX and males are XY. The term X-linked refers to genes located on the X chromosome that do not determine gender. The Y chromosome is smaller and does not carry these corresponding alleles. X-linked inheritance was discovered in the early 1900s by Thomas Hunt Morgan's group at Columbia University during experiments with fruit flies. Fruit flies make excellent laboratory models because they can be raised easily and cheaply in glass jars and share the same sex chromosome pattern as humans.

explanation: During their fruit fly experiments, Thomas Hunt Morgan's team noticed that while eye color inheritance followed a general 3:1 dominant-to-recessive ratio, only male flies expressed the white-eyed phenotype. This occurred because the eye color gene is X-linked. Because males only have a single X chromosome (XY), they have only one copy of X-linked genes. Males are therefore called hemizygous for these traits, meaning any recessive allele on their single X chromosome will be expressed.

explanation: There are several notable X-linked recessive disorders in humans. In color blindness, the gene for the blue-sensitive pigment is autosomal, but the genes for red- and green-sensitive pigments are on the X chromosome. Menkes syndrome is caused by an X-linked defective allele that disrupts copper transport in and out of cells, leading to symptoms like kinky hair, poor muscle tone, seizures, and low body temperature. Muscular dystrophy involves muscle wasting caused by the absence of the structural protein dystrophin. Adrenoleukodystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder where a carrier protein fails to transport an enzyme or very long-chain fatty acids into peroxisomes. Hemophilia is characterized by the absence or deficiency of clotting factor VIII or factor IX, which causes blood to clot very slowly or not at all.

original_text: X-linked Recessive Pedigree
explanation: An X-linked recessive pedigree traces traits caused by recessive alleles on the X chromosome. In these pedigrees, the trait is far more common in males than in females, affected males cannot pass the trait to their sons, and the trait typically passes from an affected grandfather through carrier daughters to grandsons.

questions.q: Why are X-linked recessive disorders far more common in males than in females?
opts: Females cannot inherit the recessive allele.
Males are hemizygous (XY) and only need one copy of the recessive allele on their single X chromosome to express the trait, while females (XX) need two.
The Y chromosome actively suppresses the dominant allele.
Sperm cells undergo more mutations than egg cells.
questions.exp: Option B is correct because males have only one X chromosome and express recessive X-linked alleles directly (hemizygous), whereas females must inherit two copies of the recessive allele (one on each X chromosome) to display the phenotype.
